title: Big-O Cheatsheet & Complexity Review
tagline: A complete interview-ready reference of time and space complexities for common data structures and sorting algorithms, plus a step-by-step method for analyzing any code block.

sections.content:
Walk into any technical interview at a software company and within the first ten minutes someone will ask you about complexity. Not because complexity analysis is the most interesting part of computer science — it is not — but because it is the **universal language** engineers use to compare algorithms. Without it, you cannot argue that your solution is better than a colleague's. With it, you can prove in seconds that a two-pointer scan beats a nested loop by a factor of `n`.

**Big-O notation** describes how an algorithm's resource consumption — time or space — grows as the input size `n` grows toward infinity. It captures only the *dominant growth factor* and deliberately ignores constants and lower-order terms. O(3n² + 50n + 7) and O(n²) are the same class because for large `n`, the `n²` term swamps everything else. This single act of abstraction — throwing away the noise — is what makes the notation so powerful: it lets you reason about algorithms without knowing anything about clock speed, memory bandwidth, or language runtime.

Big-O is always an **upper bound** on growth. You may also encounter **Ω (Omega)** notation for lower bounds, and **Θ (Theta)** for tight bounds — when the upper and lower bounds match. In interviews, Big-O is almost always the right answer to 'what is the complexity?' because interviewers want to know the worst-case scenario of your algorithm.

This chapter is a thorough reference and reasoning guide. It covers the full **complexity hierarchy** from O(1) to O(n!), a four-rule **analysis method** for reading code blocks, a complete **data structure operation cheatsheet** covering array, hash map, linked list, stack, queue, binary search tree, heap, and trie, the **sorting algorithm cheatsheet** with best/average/worst/space for all major algorithms, **space complexity** considerations including the hidden cost of the call stack, and the **time-space trade-off** that appears in nearly every real optimisation decision.

sections.title: The Growth Rate as Distance
sections.content:
Imagine `n = 1,000,000` as driving from New York to Los Angeles — roughly 4,500 km of road. Now change the algorithm and watch what happens to the distance:

**O(1)** is teleportation — destination reached regardless of `n`. **O(log n)** is a direct flight: no matter how much traffic there is, the plane follows a straight line of about 40 'work-steps'. **O(n)** is driving the freeway: 4,500 km, proportional to the distance. **O(n log n)** adds a few detours — call it 4,600 km. Manageable.

**O(n²)** is where things shatter. For n = 1,000,000, you perform n × n = 10¹² operations. At 10⁹ CPU operations per second, that is 1,000 seconds — nearly seventeen minutes — for a single call. An O(n²) sort on a list of a million names would take the time of a coffee break. On ten million names it takes three hours. **O(2ⁿ)** is not merely slow — it is computationally unthinkable for n > 60 on any hardware that exists today. At n = 60, O(2ⁿ) requires 2⁶⁰ ≈ 10¹⁸ operations — processing those at 10⁹ per second takes 31 years. At n = 100, the number of operations exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. These are not exaggerations; they are the mathematical reality that makes algorithm selection a genuine engineering discipline, not a stylistic preference.

sections.title: The Four Rules of Big-O Analysis
sections.content:
Reading any piece of code and producing its complexity is a skill built from four mechanical rules. Once internalised, these rules let you analyse a 100-line function in under a minute.

**Rule 1: Drop constants.** If an algorithm does exactly 2n + 50 operations, its Big-O is O(n). The constant factor 2 and the fixed offset 50 only matter on real hardware for small inputs — they do not affect how the runtime *scales*. O(500) → O(1). O(3n log n) → O(n log n).

**Rule 2: Drop non-dominant terms.** If the expression is O(n² + n), the n² term dominates for any n > 1, so we write O(n²). More generally, keep only the term that grows fastest. O(n³ + n² + n + 1) → O(n³).

**Rule 3: Sequential code blocks add.** A loop of n steps followed by a separate loop of n steps is O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) → O(n). The blocks do not multiply — they run one after the other, not inside each other.

**Rule 4: Nested code blocks multiply.** A loop of n steps that *contains* another loop of n steps is O(n × n) = O(n²). Three nested loops → O(n³). If the inner loop runs m steps (a different variable), it is O(n × m). If the outer and inner loops both iterate over the same array of size n, it is O(n²) unless you can prove the inner loop does fewer iterations on average (as in some amortised analyses).

**A fifth rule for recursion — the recurrence:** Recursive algorithms require solving a recurrence relation. The **Master Theorem** handles divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(nᵈ). If a < b^d → O(nᵈ). If a = b^d → O(nᵈ log n). If a > b^d → O(n^(log_b a)). Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → a=2, b=2, d=1, a = b^d → O(n log n). Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → a=1, b=2, d=0, a = b^d → O(log n).

sections.title: The Complexity Hierarchy in Detail
sections.content:
Understanding *why* each complexity class behaves the way it does is more useful than memorising the hierarchy. Here is each class with its defining characteristic and canonical example.

**O(1) — Constant.** The algorithm always takes the same number of steps regardless of input size. Array index access (`arr[i]`), hash map lookup, stack push/pop, and reading the head of a queue are all O(1). The key characteristic: there is no loop or recursion that scales with input.

**O(log n) — Logarithmic.** The algorithm repeatedly divides the remaining work in half (or by any constant factor). Binary search discards half the array on each comparison. A balanced binary search tree traversal descends one level at a time, and the height of a balanced tree is `log₂(n)`. Logarithms grow so slowly that `log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30`. This is the defining property of divide-and-conquer algorithms that do O(1) work per level.

**O(n) — Linear.** The algorithm visits every element of the input at most a constant number of times. A single `for` loop, building a prefix sum, linear scan for a maximum value — all O(n). If you must touch every element at least once, O(n) is optimal — you cannot do better without additional information.

**O(n log n) — Linearithmic.** This is the comparison-sort barrier. No comparison-based sort can do better than Ω(n log n) in the worst case — a fact proved by the decision tree lower bound argument. Merge sort and heap sort achieve this bound exactly. Practically, O(n log n) feels almost as fast as O(n) for up to tens of millions of elements.

**O(n²) — Quadratic.** Two nested loops, each dependent on n. Selection sort, insertion sort worst-case, naive string-matching, and all-pairs problems fall here. For n = 10,000, this is 100 million operations — borderline for a real-time system. For n = 1,000,000, it becomes intractable.

**O(2ⁿ) — Exponential.** Computing all subsets of n elements (2ⁿ subsets), naive Fibonacci (each call spawns two), most backtracking algorithms without pruning. Adding one more element to the input *doubles* the work. Feasible only for n up to roughly 20–30.

**O(n!) — Factorial.** Generating all permutations of n elements. For n = 20, n! ≈ 2.4 × 10¹⁸ — far beyond any computer. Only useful for theoretical completeness and as a worst-case baseline when discussing branch-and-bound improvements.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Each function isolates one complexity class. Binary search halves the space on every iteration — 1 billion elements need at most 30 comparisons. Merge sort's recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) solves to O(n log n) by the Master Theorem. The memoised Fibonacci replaces an exponential call tree with a linear scan of unique subproblems — the fundamental insight behind dynamic programming.

sections.title: Data Structure Operation Cheatsheet
sections.content:
Every data structure involves a set of fundamental operations — access, search, insert, delete — and their complexities determine which structure fits which problem. The complexities below are for the standard implementations; deviations exist for specialised variants.

**Array (unsorted):** Access O(1) — index arithmetic gives the address directly. Search O(n) — must scan. Insert/Delete O(n) — shifting elements maintains contiguous layout. Append to end is amortised O(1) in dynamic arrays (JavaScript `push`).

**Array (sorted):** Access O(1). Search O(log n) via binary search. Insert/Delete O(n) — binary search finds the position in O(log n) but shifting still costs O(n). The O(n) shift cost is why sorted arrays are read-heavy structures.

**Hash Map (unordered_map, dict, Map, HashMap):** Insert / Delete / Search all O(1) *average*. The hash function maps a key to a bucket index in O(1); the bucket is then scanned (typically a linked list or open-addressing probe). Worst case is O(n) when all keys collide into one bucket — pathological with a bad hash function or adversarial input. In practice, amortised O(1) is reliable with a good hash and a load factor under 0.75.

**Singly Linked List:** Access O(n) — must traverse from head. Search O(n). Insert at head O(1). Delete at head O(1). Insert/Delete at arbitrary position O(n) to reach the node, then O(1) for the pointer surgery. Doubly linked lists add a `prev` pointer for O(1) delete given a node reference (used in LRU cache implementations).

**Stack:** Push O(1), Pop O(1), Peek O(1). All three are constant because they only touch the top. Search is O(n) if needed. Implemented as a dynamic array or singly linked list; the difference is constant-factor only.

**Queue (and Deque):** Enqueue O(1), Dequeue O(1), Peek O(1). Implemented efficiently with a circular buffer or doubly linked list. A naive array-backed queue with `shift()` is O(n) — a common source of accidental quadratic behaviour.

**Binary Search Tree (BST) — balanced (AVL, Red-Black):** Access / Search / Insert / Delete all O(log n). The height of a balanced BST with n nodes is Θ(log n), and every operation traverses at most one root-to-leaf path.

**BST — unbalanced / skewed:** If you insert n values in sorted order into a plain BST with no rotation, every new node becomes the rightmost child — the tree degenerates to a linked list of height n. All operations degrade to O(n). This is why production code always uses a self-balancing variant.

**Min-Heap / Max-Heap:** Insert O(log n) — append to end and bubble up. Extract-min (or max) O(log n) — swap root with last element, remove, then sift down. Peek at min/max O(1) — the root is always accessible. Build-heap from an unordered array is O(n) using the bottom-up Floyd algorithm (not O(n log n) as naive insertion-one-by-one would suggest). Search is O(n) — heaps do not support efficient arbitrary search.

**Trie (prefix tree):** Insert / Search / Delete are all O(m) where m is the length of the key (not the number of keys in the trie). Tries are length-bounded, not size-bounded — this is the key difference from trees. Ideal for autocomplete, spell-check, and IP routing tables. Space is O(n × m) in the worst case (no shared prefixes).

sections.title: Sorting Algorithm Cheatsheet
sections.content:
Sorting is one of the most studied problems in computer science, and the diversity of algorithms reflects genuinely different trade-offs between time, space, stability, and input characteristics.

**Bubble Sort — O(n²) / O(n) best / O(1) space / stable.** Repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order. On a nearly-sorted array with only a few swaps needed, it terminates early at O(n). In practice, no one uses bubble sort except as a teaching tool.

**Selection Sort — O(n²) all cases / O(1) space / unstable.** Finds the minimum of the remaining unsorted portion and places it at the front, one element per pass. Performs exactly O(n²/2) comparisons regardless of input order — not adaptive. Useful only when minimising the number of *swaps* (not comparisons) matters.

**Insertion Sort — O(n²) avg / O(n) best / O(1) space / stable.** Maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new element into its correct position. Adaptive: nearly-sorted input runs in O(n). Used as the base case in hybrid sorts (Timsort, IntroSort) for small subarrays (typically n < 16) because its low overhead beats merge sort at small scales.

**Merge Sort — O(n log n) all cases / O(n) space / stable.** Divides the array in half recursively, sorts each half, then merges. The merge step is O(n) and is repeated O(log n) times. Guaranteed O(n log n) regardless of input. The O(n) auxiliary space is its main drawback. The standard sort for external data (too large to fit in RAM) because it reads sequentially.

**Quick Sort — O(n log n) avg / O(n²) worst / O(log n) space / unstable.** Partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts each partition. With randomised pivot selection, the probability of hitting O(n²) on any input drops to negligibly small. In practice the fastest comparison sort due to cache efficiency and small constant factors. The worst case (always choosing the smallest or largest element as pivot) is avoidable with median-of-three or random pivot strategies.

**Heap Sort — O(n log n) all cases / O(1) space / unstable.** Builds a max-heap in O(n) then repeatedly extracts the maximum in O(log n). Guaranteed O(n log n) like merge sort, but O(1) extra space like insertion sort. The trade-off: poor cache performance due to non-sequential memory access patterns, so it is slower in practice than quick sort despite identical asymptotic bounds.

**Counting Sort — O(n + k) time / O(k) space / stable.** Not comparison-based — it counts the frequency of each value. Linear when k (the value range) is O(n). Useless when k >> n (e.g., sorting 64-bit integers). Ideal for sorting ages (0–120), ASCII characters (0–255), or bounded-domain categorical data.

**Radix Sort — O(d × (n + k)) time / O(n + k) space / stable.** Sorts integers digit by digit from least significant to most significant, using counting sort as a subroutine. d is the number of digits. For 32-bit integers with base 256, d = 4 and k = 256, giving O(4n) = O(n). Faster than comparison sorts for large integer arrays.

sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing a sort. The right answer depends on value range, stability requirement, and available memory.

sections.title: Space Complexity — The Dimension Engineers Forget
sections.content:
Every algorithm consumes not just time but memory. Space complexity follows the same Big-O rules as time complexity, but engineers under pressure on a whiteboard often forget to state it. An interviewer who asks 'can you do better on space?' is checking exactly this.

**Types of space to count:**

1. **Input space**: The memory taken by the input itself. Conventionally, input space is *not* counted in the algorithm's space complexity — you assume it is given. But if you copy the input, that copy counts.

2. **Auxiliary space**: The *extra* memory your algorithm allocates beyond the input — this is what 'O(1) space' means. A truly in-place algorithm allocates only a fixed number of variables regardless of `n`.

3. **Call stack space**: Recursion creates a new stack frame per call. A recursive function that calls itself n times before returning has O(n) stack space. A log-depth recursion (like merge sort's splitting phase) uses O(log n) stack space. This cost is invisible in the code but very real — deep recursion on large inputs causes stack overflow.

**Worked examples:**

- **In-place two-pointer reverse**: O(1) space — only two index variables allocated regardless of array size.
- **Merge sort**: O(n) auxiliary space for the merged arrays at each level, plus O(log n) stack space for the recursive call tree. Total: O(n).
- **Quick sort**: O(log n) space for the call stack (average, with balanced partitioning), O(n) worst case (maximally unbalanced partition).
- **DFS on a graph**: O(V) space for the visited set and the call stack (depth up to V nodes).
- **BFS on a graph**: O(V) space for the queue — in the worst case (star graph) the queue holds all nodes at once.
- **Hash map to deduplicate**: O(n) space — the set grows linearly with the number of distinct elements.

**The classic time-space trade-off** appears everywhere: pay O(n) extra space to buy O(n) faster time. The canonical example is duplicate detection — O(n²) brute force with O(1) space, or O(n) with a hash set at O(n) space. Neither is strictly better; the right answer depends on your memory budget. Recognising and articulating this trade-off explicitly is a hallmark of an experienced engineer.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The recursive sum creates n stack frames — one per element — before any frame can be freed. For 100,000 elements, this crashes in most runtimes. The divide-and-conquer version splits the problem log-depth, so the stack only grows to log₂(100000) ≈ 17 frames. The Two Sum hash map example is the canonical interview demonstration that O(n) space buys you a factor-of-n speedup.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Interview Pitfalls
sections.content:
After hundreds of interview cycles, the same mistakes appear repeatedly. Knowing these ahead of time lets you avoid them.

**Misconception 1: 'Two nested loops always means O(n²).'** Not quite. If the inner loop has a fixed bound that does not scale with n — for example, always iterating over 26 letters of the alphabet — it contributes a constant factor, and the overall complexity is O(n), not O(n²). Similarly, if the inner loop's bound decreases as the outer loop progresses (such as the right pointer in a two-pointer algorithm), the total iterations may still be O(n).

**Misconception 2: 'Big-O is the worst case.'** Big-O is an *upper bound*, not necessarily the worst case. An algorithm can have an O(n) upper bound but run in O(1) in the best case (e.g., linear search finds the target at position 0). When people say 'time complexity' without qualification, they typically mean worst-case Big-O, but be precise in interviews.

**Misconception 3: 'O(n log n) is always better than O(n²).'** Asymptotically yes, but for small n, the constant factors can reverse the ranking. Insertion sort beats merge sort for arrays under ~16 elements in practice — which is why Timsort and IntroSort switch to insertion sort for small partitions. However, unless you have profiler data showing n stays small, always prefer the better asymptotic bound.

**Misconception 4: 'Space complexity just counts what I allocate.'** Many candidates forget the call stack. A DFS that recurses n levels deep uses O(n) space even if it allocates no variables inside the recursive function. Always trace the maximum recursion depth.

**Misconception 5: 'Average case equals amortised.'** Average case is the expected performance over random inputs. Amortised is the average cost per operation over a *sequence* of operations, regardless of input distribution. Dynamic array push is O(1) amortised — any single push is O(1) except when doubling occurs (O(n)), but the total cost of n pushes is O(n). These are different concepts.

**Misconception 6: 'Hash map operations are O(1).'** Always qualify with 'average' or 'amortised.' Hash maps have O(n) worst case when all keys hash to the same bucket. In most production settings with a good hash function this is irrelevant, but in competitive programming with adversarial inputs (or when using languages with predictable hash functions), hash collisions can be deliberately triggered, degrading performance. Sorted maps (tree-backed) guarantee O(log n) worst case.

sections.title: Amortised Analysis: When Individual Operations Lie
sections.content:
Some data structures have operations that are occasionally expensive but cheap on average over a sequence of calls. **Amortised analysis** accounts for this by spreading the cost of expensive operations across many cheap ones.

The canonical example is the **dynamic array** (JavaScript array, Python list, Java ArrayList). When the internal buffer is full, the array doubles in capacity — an O(n) copy. But this doubling happens exponentially rarely: after the first copy (at capacity 1), the next is at 2, then 4, then 8. The total cost of n pushes is 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … + n ≈ 2n, so the *amortised* cost per push is O(1). Stating that `push` is O(n) would be technically true for the worst single call but deeply misleading for any sequence of calls.

**The banker's method** is one formal way to prove amortised bounds: assign each O(1) push a 'credit' of 2 units. When a copy happens, use the stored credits to pay for it. If the credits always cover the expensive operations, the amortised cost is bounded.

Other amortised-O(1) examples: splay tree operations (amortised O(log n) per operation over a sequence), union-find (amortised O(α(n)) with path compression and union by rank, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively a constant for any practical n), and queue implemented with two stacks (amortised O(1) dequeue).

In interviews, it is fine to say 'O(1) amortised' for dynamic array push. If pressed, explain the doubling strategy and total cost argument — it demonstrates mathematical maturity.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Choosing Complexity in Practice
sections.content:
Academic complexity analysis and production engineering sometimes diverge. Here is how to bridge the two.

**When O(n²) is acceptable:** For n < 1000, an O(n²) algorithm typically runs in under 1 ms even in interpreted languages. If n is bounded by a small constant in your domain — say, the number of columns in a database table (rarely more than 200) — O(n²) is fine and the simpler code is preferable. The YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) principle applies: do not optimise prematurely.

**When O(n log n) is the practical ceiling for user-facing operations:** Any algorithm that a user waits for interactively should be O(n log n) or better. 100 ms is the threshold of 'instant' for humans; at 10⁹ ops/sec, that is 10⁸ operations. For n = 1,000,000, O(n log n) ≈ 20M operations — well within budget. O(n²) ≈ 10¹² — hopelessly over.

**When O(n) is achievable with a hash map trade-off:** The most common interview optimisation is replacing a brute-force O(n²) nested search with an O(n) hash map single pass. Two Sum, subarray sum equals k, grouping anagrams, longest substring without repeating characters — all follow this pattern. The trade-off is O(n) space for the hash map.

**When the constant factor matters more than the class:** Sorting 10,000 integers — both O(n²) insertion sort and O(n log n) merge sort are fine, and in practice insertion sort may be faster due to cache behaviour and smaller code size. At 100 million integers, merge sort wins by a large margin. Know your n.

**Graph algorithms** are their own complexity family. BFS and DFS are O(V + E) — linear in the number of vertices and edges. Dijkstra's shortest path with a priority queue is O((V + E) log V). Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path is O(V³). When edges are sparse (E ≈ V), these simplify; when dense (E ≈ V²), they degrade.

**Historical context:** Big-O notation was introduced by the German mathematician Paul Bachmann in his 1894 book on analytic number theory, and popularised by Edmund Landau — which is why it is sometimes called Bachmann-Landau notation. Donald Knuth standardised its use in computer science in *The Art of Computer Programming* (1968) and introduced the Ω and Θ notations to complete the picture. The notation predates computers by decades; it was originally used to describe the growth of number-theoretic functions. Knuth's contribution was applying it to describe algorithm resource usage — a framing so powerful that it became the universal language of algorithm analysis.

**Interview checklist — state both dimensions every time.** When you present a solution, always say: 'The time complexity is O(X) because Y, and the space complexity is O(Z) because W.' Common traps: (1) forgetting the call stack for recursive solutions — a DFS solution is O(V) space, not O(1); (2) citing O(n) time but forgetting to mention the O(n) hash map cost; (3) saying 'the sort is O(n log n)' without noting whether you are sorting in-place or creating a copy. Interviewers award points for correctly identifying the space dimension — it is a reliable differentiator between candidates who have thought carefully versus those who memorised formulas.

items: **Drop constants and lower-order terms.** O(3n² + 5n + 100) is O(n²). O(2n) is O(n). Only the dominant growth factor survives.
**Nested loops multiply; sequential loops add.** Two back-to-back O(n) loops is O(n). One O(n) loop inside another O(n) loop is O(n²). Three nested loops is O(n³).
**Halving the input each step → O(log n).** Binary search and balanced BST operations are canonical. log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30 — logarithms are extraordinarily powerful.
**Hash maps trade O(n) space for O(1) average-time lookup.** The most frequent brute-force-to-optimal upgrade in interviews: replace an O(n²) nested search with one O(n) pass using a hash set or map.

**Sorting cheatsheet:** Merge sort — O(n log n) all cases, stable, O(n) space. Quick sort — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, O(log n) space. Heap sort — O(n log n) all cases, O(1) space, unstable. Counting/Radix — O(n) but require bounded value range.
**Call stack space is real space.** Linear recursion → O(n) stack. Divide-and-conquer (log-depth) → O(log n) stack. Always trace the maximum recursion depth when quoting space complexity.

**Amortised O(1) is not the same as worst-case O(1).** Dynamic array push, union-find operations, and queue-from-two-stacks are amortised constant — any single call can be expensive, but the average over a sequence is O(1).

**State both time and space.** In every interview answer, quote both dimensions explicitly. The space cost of a hash map or the stack cost of a recursion is exactly what interviewers probe with follow-up questions.

quiz.question: What is the Big-O simplification of O(4n² + 12n + 200)?
options: O(4n²)
O(n² + n)
O(n²)
O(n)
quiz.explanation: Drop the constant multiplier (4) and all lower-order terms (12n + 200). The dominant term is n², so the simplified Big-O is O(n²). Constants never affect the asymptotic class.

quiz.question: A function has three separate sequential loops each iterating n times. What is the total time complexity?
options: O(n³) — three loops multiply.
O(3n) — three loops add.
O(n) — drop the constant coefficient.
O(n log n) — multiple passes create a log factor.
quiz.explanation: Sequential (non-nested) loops add their costs: O(n) + O(n) + O(n) = O(3n). Dropping the constant coefficient gives O(n). Multiplication only occurs when loops are nested inside each other.

quiz.question: Binary search on a sorted array of 1 billion elements requires at most how many comparisons?
quiz.explanation: Binary search is O(log₂ n). log₂(1,000,000,000) ≈ 30. Each comparison halves the remaining search space, so 30 halvings cover 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 billion items. This is the power of logarithmic algorithms.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a reason why hash map operations are sometimes stated as O(n) worst case?
options: All keys hash to the same bucket, forming a linked list.
Adversarial input is crafted to trigger maximum collisions.
The hash map needs to resize, copying all entries.
The hash function itself takes O(n) time to compute for length-n string keys.
quiz.explanation: Resizing (rehashing) is an O(n) operation, but it is amortised across many insertions — it does not make individual operations O(n) in the amortised sense. The other three options are genuine causes of O(n) worst case for a single operation: bucket collision chains, adversarial inputs, and long key hashing.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm guarantees O(n log n) in ALL cases (best, average, and worst) while using O(1) extra space?
options: Merge Sort
Quick Sort
Heap Sort
Counting Sort
quiz.explanation: Heap Sort is O(n log n) in all three cases and sorts in-place using O(1) extra space. Merge sort is O(n log n) always but needs O(n) auxiliary space. Quick sort degrades to O(n²) worst case. Counting sort is O(n + k) but requires O(k) space and is not comparison-based.

quiz.question: A recursive function calls itself once per element with no early return. What is its call stack space complexity?
options: O(1) — stack frames are reused.
O(log n) — recursion is always logarithmic.
O(n) — one stack frame per element before any unwind.
O(n²) — each frame duplicates the previous.
quiz.explanation: Linear recursion (one call per element, no branching) creates n stack frames that all coexist on the call stack before the first can be freed. This is O(n) space — regardless of what each frame does. Stack overflow occurs for large n in most runtimes.

quiz.question: Inserting elements in strictly ascending order into a plain (non-self-balancing) Binary Search Tree results in:
options: A perfectly balanced tree — sorted input is optimal for BSTs.
A skewed tree equivalent to a linked list, degrading all operations to O(n).
Automatic rebalancing triggered by the BST invariant.
A tree of height O(log n) due to the sorted property.
quiz.explanation: Inserting sorted values into a plain BST creates a completely right-skewed tree where every node has only a right child — structurally identical to a linked list with height n. All operations (search, insert, delete) degrade to O(n). Self-balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black) prevent this via rotations.

quiz.question: Which statement about the time-space trade-off in duplicate detection is most accurate?
options: The O(n) hash set approach is strictly better than the O(n log n) sort-then-scan approach.
The sort-then-scan approach is strictly better because it uses less space.
Both O(n) time/O(n) space and O(n log n) time/O(1) space are valid; the best choice depends on memory constraints.
Neither is correct — duplicates can always be found in O(1) time.
quiz.explanation: Both approaches are legitimate with different trade-offs: O(n) time with O(n) hash set space, or O(n log n) time with O(1) space by sorting in-place then scanning adjacent elements. Recognising this trade-off — neither solution dominates the other — is the mature engineering answer.

quiz.question: Counting Sort runs in O(n + k) time. What is k?
options: The number of distinct elements in the input.
The log of the maximum value.
The range of possible values (max − min + 1).
The number of comparisons made.
quiz.explanation: Counting Sort allocates a frequency array of size k = max − min + 1. It works by counting occurrences of each value, then reconstructing the sorted order. It is efficient when k is small relative to n (e.g., sorting ages 0–120 or byte values 0–255). When k >> n, the space and initialisation cost dominates.

quiz.question: A divide-and-conquer algorithm splits the problem in half at each level and does O(n) work per level. According to the Master Theorem, its time complexity is:
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
quiz.explanation: This matches the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) — merge sort's recurrence. In Master Theorem terms: a=2, b=2, d=1. Since a = b^d (2 = 2¹), the complexity is O(nᵈ log n) = O(n log n). The O(n) merge work is done across O(log n) levels of recursion, giving O(n log n) total.
